title: Buffer Manager and 2Q Replacement
subtitle: Turn page requests into safe, concurrent access to a bounded in-memory buffer while preserving dirty data.
assignment_brief: Implement a buffer manager for configurable page and buffer sizes. A 64-bit page identifier uses its high 16 bits as the segment id and its low 48 bits as the page number inside that segment; each segment is persisted in a file named by the segment id.

fix_page(page_id, exclusive) must return a resident frame protected in shared or exclusive mode, loading the page on a miss. unfix_page(frame, dirty) releases the caller's fix and records modifications. When no free frame remains, a 2Q-style FIFO/LRU policy must choose an unfixed victim or throw buffer_full_error.

The concurrency requirement is part of the algorithm, not an optional optimization: unrelated page requests must continue while one thread waits for a page latch, and the global manager latch must not cover slow disk I/O.
learning_outcomes: Trace a buffer hit, buffer miss, dirty eviction, and buffer-full failure while preserving the page-table and pin-count invariants.
Simulate the assignment's two-list replacement policy and explain why one-time scan pages stay separate from pages that demonstrate reuse.
Explain the different jobs of the page table, buffer frame, pin count, dirty flag, replacement metadata, page latch, manager mutex, and per-segment file latch.
Write deadlock-aware fix/unfix pseudocode that releases the global manager mutex before ordinary page-latch waits and disk I/O.
Separate buffer-manager durability from transaction recovery: writing dirty pages is necessary, but WAL/LSNs are outside this exercise.

concepts.title: Resident pages, frames, and the page table
concepts.takeaway: A page is a persistent logical block; a frame is one reusable memory slot that currently contains some page.
explanation: The manager preallocates page_count frames, each with page_size bytes. page_table maps a full 64-bit page id to the frame that currently contains it, so a buffer hit is expected O(1). Frame identity is stable, but its page_id and bytes change after eviction; callers must not retain or use get_data() after the final unfix.

The page id is split as [16-bit segment id | 48-bit segment-local page id]. The segment selects a file; the local page id multiplied by page_size gives the byte offset. A page beyond the current file end is returned as an all-zero page.
pseudocode: segment_id       := page_id >> 48
segment_page_id  := page_id & ((1 << 48) - 1)
offset           := segment_page_id * page_size
if file_size < offset + page_size: return zero_page
else: read page_size bytes at offset
invariants: Every resident page has exactly one page-table entry.
Every resident frame is in exactly one replacement queue: FIFO or LRU.
A frame with fix_count > 0 cannot be selected as a victim.
The frame's bytes are valid for the advertised page_id before another thread can acquire its page latch.
pitfalls: Confusing a page id with a frame number.
Using a frame's data after unfix, when the frame may already have been reused.
Forgetting that offset multiplication can overflow for hostile page_size/page_id inputs; this student implementation performs no explicit overflow check.

source_refs.note: Defines 2Q, 64-bit page ids, segment layout, configurable sizes, and concurrent fix/unfix.
Declares frame state, page table, queues, segment files, API, and page-id split helpers.
Preallocates frame storage and implements segment-offset reads with zero-fill beyond EOF.

concepts.title: The assignment's FIFO/LRU form of 2Q
concepts.takeaway: Give new pages one FIFO chance; only pages requested again earn space in the recency-managed hot queue.
explanation: A miss inserts the page at the FIFO tail. A hit on a FIFO page promotes it to the LRU tail; a hit on an LRU page refreshes it to the tail. Victim selection scans from the FIFO head for the first unfixed frame, then from the LRU head.

This resists scan pollution: pages touched once remain eviction candidates, while a reused index root reaches the hot queue. For exam answers, call this the course/assignment variant of 2Q. Canonical published 2Q is often described with queue-size targets and an A1out ghost-history queue, neither of which exists here.
pseudocode: on MISS(page): load page; FIFO.push_back(frame)
on HIT(frame in FIFO): FIFO.erase(frame); LRU.push_back(frame)
on HIT(frame in LRU): move frame to LRU.back
victim := first frame in FIFO with fix_count = 0
if none: victim := first frame in LRU with fix_count = 0
if none: throw buffer_full_error
invariants: Newly loaded pages enter FIFO.
A resident page's second request promotes it from FIFO to LRU.
The front of each queue is the first eviction candidate within that queue.
Fixed frames stay in their queue but are skipped during victim selection.
pitfalls: Calling this a complete implementation of every canonical 2Q variant; it has no ghost queue or explicit queue-size partition.
Evicting the queue head without checking fix_count.
Updating queue metadata without the manager mutex.
Assuming promotion occurs on unfix: this implementation updates recency when fix_page observes the hit.

source_refs.note: Implements queue transitions and FIFO-first victim search.
Promotes hits and inserts newly loaded frames into FIFO.
Specifies FIFO eviction, second-access promotion, and LRU refresh order.

concepts.title: Fix, latch, dirty, and unfix
concepts.takeaway: Pinning prevents replacement; latching controls concurrent byte access; dirty state decides whether replacement needs a write.
explanation: fix_count is the replacement pin count. page_mutex is the data-access latch: shared fixes may coexist, while an exclusive fix excludes all other access. dirty is sticky until a successful write path resets or removes the frame, so any unfix marked dirty makes later eviction/destruction write the page.

The interface does not pass the original lock mode to unfix_page. This solution therefore stores, per thread and per frame, the mode and recursive fix count. That supports repeated same-mode fixes without recursively locking std::shared_mutex. It does not correctly upgrade a nested shared fix to exclusive; the implementation returns early without checking the new exclusive request.
pseudocode: FIX(page, mode): increment global fix_count before waiting for page latch
if this thread already fixed frame: increment local nesting count; return
acquire frame latch in requested mode
remember {local_count = 1, original_mode}
UNFIX(frame, dirty): frame.dirty := frame.dirty OR dirty
if local_count > 1: decrement local_count and fix_count
else: unlock in remembered mode; erase local record; decrement fix_count
invariants: fix_count counts all outstanding fixes, including nested fixes.
A thread unlocks in the same shared/exclusive mode it originally acquired.
Dirty state is monotonic between load and write-back.
The last local unfix releases the page latch and one unit of fix_count.
pitfalls: Treating pinning and latching as the same mechanism.
Forgetting to mark a modified page dirty.
Attempting a shared-to-exclusive nested upgrade: the current code silently keeps only the shared latch.
Returning from a thread without balancing every fix; neither the latch nor fix_count is repaired automatically.
Calling unfix_page from a different thread: the thread-local record is absent and this implementation silently returns.

source_refs.note: Shows distinct dirty, fix-count, and page-latch state plus the public lifecycle contract.
Tracks lock mode and nesting per thread; the early return at 243-245 exposes the unsupported upgrade case.
Pinned frames cannot be evicted, and exclusive page access serializes concurrent increments.

concepts.title: Miss handling and dirty eviction
concepts.takeaway: Reserve and protect a frame under metadata synchronization, then perform slow write/read work after releasing the global manager mutex.
explanation: On a miss, the manager chooses an unused frame or an unfixed victim. It exclusively latches that frame, remembers a dirty victim's old page id, removes the old mapping, installs the new page's metadata and FIFO entry, and increments fix_count—all while holding manager_mutex.

After manager_mutex is released, a dirty old page is written, the requested page is read, and the exclusive frame latch is retained or converted to shared for the caller. Publishing the page-table entry before I/O is safe because other fixers increment the pin and then block on the frame latch; they cannot observe half-loaded bytes.
pseudocode: lock manager
if unused frame exists: frame := unused frame
else: frame := FIFO/LRU victim with fix_count = 0; lock frame exclusively
remember old {page_id, dirty}; erase old page-table and queue entries
install new {page_id, fix_count = 1, dirty = false}; FIFO.push(frame); page_table[new] := frame
unlock manager
if old dirty: write old bytes to old page id
read requested page into frame
return with exclusive latch, or convert to shared
invariants: The dirty old bytes are written using the old page id before the frame data is overwritten.
No caller can observe a partly loaded page.
The global manager mutex is not held during disk I/O.
A miss-in-progress is pinned and therefore cannot itself become a victim.
pitfalls: Overwriting the victim before writing its dirty bytes.
Holding manager_mutex during disk I/O and serializing unrelated requests.
Ignoring I/O exceptions: this solution uses raw latch lock/unlock and publishes new metadata before I/O, so a thrown open/read/write error can leave the frame latched and the mapping inconsistent.

source_refs.note: Complete hit/miss path, victim reservation, dirty write-back, read, and latch handoff.
Requires deadlock resistance and short global latch hold times around millisecond-scale I/O.
Checks persistence and that waiting on one page does not block unrelated page operations.

concepts.title: Segment files and resize coordination
concepts.takeaway: Cache one File object per segment and synchronize its cached size so block I/O remains race-free.
explanation: README warns that separate File objects referring to the same file are unsafe. segment_files therefore caches one SegmentFile per 16-bit segment id. A short file_mutex protects only lookup/creation of this map.

Each SegmentFile has a cached size and shared_mutex. Reads and in-range writes hold a shared lock, which allows the File API's thread-safe pread/pwrite calls to overlap. Extending the file uses an exclusive lock and a second size check. The global manager mutex is never needed for this work.
pseudocode: sf := get_or_create_single_segment_file(segment_id)
shared_lock sf
if sf.size >= required_size: write block; return
unlock shared; exclusive_lock sf
if sf.size < required_size: resize; sf.size := required_size
unlock exclusive; shared_lock sf; write block
invariants: At most one cached File object represents a segment within the manager.
The cached size is read or changed under that segment's mutex.
Resize is exclusive; block reads/writes may proceed concurrently once the size is sufficient.
Different segment files need not share one long-lived I/O latch.
pitfalls: Opening a new File object on every page request.
Checking size concurrently with resize without synchronization.
Claiming that the implementation holds no latch during I/O: it intentionally holds the frame latch and a per-segment shared latch, while avoiding the global manager latch.

source_refs.note: States that only block reads/writes are thread-safe and duplicate File objects are unsafe.
Specifies size/resize versus block-read/write thread-safety.
Implements the cached file, size checks, double-checked growth, and block I/O.

trace.title: A scan page loses to a reused page, and a dirty victim is written
trace.setup: Use three frames. All pages are initially absent. Show queues from oldest to newest and assume every fix is followed by unfix.
steps: Fix 1: miss; load it and place it in FIFO. State: FIFO [1], LRU [].
Fix 1 again: hit; promote it to the LRU tail. State: FIFO [2], LRU [1].
Fix 3 exclusively, modify it, and unfix dirty. State: FIFO [2, 3], LRU [1]; page 3 is dirty.
Fix 4: the pool is full. Victim search starts at FIFO and evicts clean page 2. State after load: FIFO [3, 4], LRU [1].

Fix 5: FIFO is preferred again, so dirty page 3 is selected. While its frame is exclusively latched, write page 3 to its segment file, then read page 5 into the same frame. Final state: FIFO [4, 5], LRU [1].
trace.result: The once-touched pages churn through FIFO, the reused page 1 remains protected in LRU, and dirty data is persisted before frame reuse.

decisions.title: Store frame pointers and queue iterators
decisions.rationale: Victim scans inspect fix_count directly, and a frame can be erased from its queue in O(1) without a second page-table lookup.
decisions.tradeoff: Queue iterators and queue_type become metadata invariants that every transition must update consistently.

source_refs.note: Stores replacement membership on each frame and frame pointers in both queues.
Report rationale agrees with the final implementation and git commit f08255b.

decisions.title: Release manager_mutex before page-latch waits and I/O
decisions.rationale: One contested page or slow device request must not prevent threads from looking up and fixing unrelated pages.
decisions.tradeoff: The miss path must publish carefully ordered metadata and use the frame latch as the completion barrier for other requesters.

source_refs.note: The manager-lock scope ends before I/O and before ordinary hit-path latch acquisition.
Exercises progress on page 1 while another thread waits for page 0.

decisions.title: Use atomics for dirty and fix_count
decisions.rationale: unfix_page can record dirtiness and release a pin without reacquiring the global manager mutex; victim selection reads the pin count while holding manager_mutex.
decisions.tradeoff: Correctness now depends on a subtle ordering protocol across the frame latch, manager mutex, and relaxed atomics; atomics alone do not make queue metadata safe.

source_refs.note: dirty and fix_count are atomic, while queues remain protected metadata.
Victim selection reads fix_count and unfix updates dirty/pins without manager_mutex.

decisions.title: Cache and separately latch segment files
decisions.rationale: It obeys the File API's single-object requirement and lets unrelated segments progress independently.
decisions.tradeoff: The manager carries a persistent open-file cache and a two-level file_mutex/per-segment-mutex protocol.

source_refs.note: Implements map-level creation protection and segment-local size/I/O coordination.
The retrospective description matches the checked implementation.

drills.prompt: Write fix_page miss-path pseudocode that is safe under concurrent requests for the same missing page.
drills.answer: Under the manager mutex choose and exclusively latch an unused/unpinned frame, remove the old mapping, install the requested page's mapping with fix_count 1 and FIFO membership, then release the manager mutex. Write the dirty victim if needed and read the new page while retaining the frame latch. A second requester may find the published mapping and increment fix_count, but must block on that latch until loading completes.
checklist: Remember the old page id before overwriting metadata.
Publish one page-table entry and one queue membership.
Use the frame latch to hide partial loading.

drills.prompt: Simulate FIFO and LRU after the reference string 1, 2, 1, 3, 4 with three frames under this assignment's policy.
drills.answer: After 1: FIFO [1], LRU []. After 2: FIFO [1,2]. The second 1 promotes it: FIFO [2], LRU [1]. After 3: FIFO [2,3], LRU [1]. Request 4 evicts FIFO head 2, so FIFO [3,4], LRU [1].
checklist: A hit on FIFO promotes to LRU.
Queue order is oldest to newest.

drills.prompt: Why are fix_count and page_mutex both necessary?
drills.answer: fix_count protects residency: replacement skips any frame an operator is using. page_mutex protects the bytes: many readers may share it, but a writer needs exclusive access. A page can be unfixed yet remain resident, and a fixed page still needs a latch mode, so neither mechanism substitutes for the other.
checklist: Shared reader and exclusive writer behavior.

drills.prompt: Debug this sequence in the submitted implementation: one thread calls fix_page(P, false), then fix_page(P, true) before either unfix.
drills.answer: The second call finds the frame in the thread-local map, increments only the local nesting count, and returns without upgrading the shared latch. The caller therefore does not receive the requested exclusive protection. A correct design must reject upgrades, provide an explicit safe upgrade protocol, or define that nested fixes must use a compatible mode.
checklist: Locate the early return at src/buffer_manager.cc:241-245.
Explain why shared-to-exclusive cannot be silently treated as shared.

drills.prompt: Compare this implementation with canonical 2Q descriptions.
drills.answer: Both separate first-touch pages from reused hot pages. This assignment uses a resident FIFO plus resident LRU and always searches FIFO first. Canonical 2Q is commonly described with capacity tuning and an A1out ghost queue that remembers recently evicted first-touch pages. Do not invent that ghost queue when tracing the submitted code, and do not generalize the code as the only form of 2Q.
checklist: Answer according to the variant named in the question.

drills.prompt: Does flushing every dirty victim make this buffer manager transactionally crash-safe?
drills.answer: No. Dirty write-back preserves page bytes across replacement, but a transactional DBMS must also enforce write-ahead logging, track page/log sequence information, and support undo/redo according to its steal/force policy. This exercise's BufferFrame has no page LSN and implements no log protocol.

limitations: README and tests define the assignment contract. The implementation is student work and the report is a later retrospective; neither should be presented as course ground truth.
The implementation is the assignment's simplified resident FIFO/LRU form of 2Q, not every canonical 2Q variant; it has no A1out ghost queue or explicit queue-size target.
Nested same-thread shared-to-exclusive fix upgrades are not supported correctly, and the public contract does not document that limitation.
The raw lock/unlock miss path is not exception-safe: an I/O/open/resize failure after metadata publication can leave a frame latched and the page table inconsistent.
Destructor write-back assumes the manager is no longer used concurrently. No page latches are acquired while collecting/writing dirty frames.
No WAL, page LSN, transaction commit/abort, background writer, explicit flush API, or recovery protocol is implemented.

The provided gtests were inspected but not rerun in this audit because the legacy CMake build downloads external GoogleTest/benchmark dependencies. Both core implementation translation units compiled warning-free with C++20 locally.

verified_report_claims: The page-id split, page-table/frame layout, FIFO/LRU transitions, cached segment files, per-segment shared mutex, thread-local fix tracking, and global-lock/I/O separation all match the final source.
The report's named implementation commits exist in git history, including segmenting files, pointer queues, the fix_page rework, and shared_mutex.
The report's test summaries match the assertions in test/buffer_manager_test.cc.
corrections_to_report: The report says thread-local tracking supports repeated fixes, but it does not qualify that a nested shared-to-exclusive mode change is silently not upgraded.

The shorthand 'do not hold latches during I/O' must be taught as 'do not hold the global manager latch during I/O.' The code intentionally holds the frame latch and a per-segment shared latch during I/O.
The report calls the design 2Q without noting that the exercise implements a simplified two-resident-queue variant rather than the ghost-queue form often described in literature.
Stress tests are evidence of observed behavior, not a proof that no race or deadlock can exist.

implementation_findings.finding: A nested shared-to-exclusive fix returns without upgrading the latch.
A throwing dirty write or page read after page-table publication can strand the raw frame latch and an invalid mapping.
The code has resident FIFO and LRU lists but no ghost queue or explicit target sizes.
Dirty write-back is implemented without page LSN or WAL coordination, so it must not be taught as transactional recovery.
